DataCurrent figures are rewritten from their measurement on every build and checked by the verifier the report describes. Historical figures come from git, up to commit 8cecf4b4 (2026-10-07, 17:58 UTC), and from the issue tracker. Abstract

Coding agents produce code faster than a person can review it, and each change can break an invariant that nobody planned for. Verified Agentic Engineering (VAE) moves part of the definition of done from the prompt into programs. An instruction file states the project's conventions; a deterministic verifier, written by the coding agent, checks the conventions encoded in its rules and prints a fix for each failure. The harness returns the verifier's diagnostics to the agent, and a failing gate blocks the commit. Lessons from each session become tests, verifier rules or memory lines, and a person reviews every change before release. This report covers one case: defuss-shadcn, a standalone HTML component system forked at 55 components and developed by one maintainer with one model family from 2026-09-05 to 2026-10-07, with 220 commits and 17 releases, growing to 232 components. Of the lines added to components, tests, the shared runtime and the theme, 4.9 % were removed later. In one session, four changes reached every module: typed API documentation for all 59 interactive components (four hours, one human correction), unit-test line coverage from 31.6 % to 75.6 % (21 minutes), every component folder moved under a new layout gate (43 minutes), and 1,147 type errors removed with the shipped files byte-identical (27 minutes). The study has no control group, so it cannot isolate the method's effect, and the gates missed defects that a person or a clean machine found.

1Introduction

A prompt can ask an agent to run the tests, to avoid mocks and to remove its debug output. It cannot make the agent comply, and the next session starts without the lessons of the last one. An agent that changes hundreds of files a day does not wait for review, so any promise a project makes - every state reachable by name, every color taken from a design token, every example showing the code that renders it - tends to erode unless a program checks it.

VAE is built on that premise. This report is a case study, not a benchmark: one project, one maintainer, one model family, 33 days. The repository and the recorded measurements are public. The study has no control group, so it cannot isolate the method's effect. The current figures on this page are rewritten from their measurements on every build, and the build fails when a figure and its measurement disagree. Material claims carry one of three tags, defined in section 3: VERIFIED for direct evidence, HYPOTHESIS for a testable inference with its falsifier, UNKNOWN for what the evidence does not settle.

2The method

defuss-vae packages the method for Claude Code, Codex and other harnesses that load Agent Skills: seven skills, three hooks and a set of Python programs that use only the standard library. The agent does the work; the gate decides whether it may be committed. VERIFIED (defuss-vae 0.8.0 source) This section describes release 0.8.0 of 2026-10-07.

2.1 Gating slop

The method reaches the harness through three hooks. At session start one injects the rules, the agent's memory and its open leads (section 2.3). When the agent tries to end its turn, the second runs the gate and, while the gate is open, sends the agent back once with the gate's instructions. The third denies git commit until the fingerprint of the changed files has passed three steps. Verify runs the project's own commands - lint, unit tests, coverage, end-to-end tests - and the rules in .agents/VERIFY.py. Review requires an attestation for the same fingerprint: a 16-point checklist, every changed path, and every finding resolved, with what it taught recorded as a test, a verifier rule, a memory line or nothing. Docs requires a second attestation that records why the design beats a plausible alternative.

The gate fails closed: a missing command or a metric it cannot parse counts as UNKNOWN, UNKNOWN blocks, and an error inside the gate itself denies the commit. Verified has a fixed meaning. Lint passes; tests pass against real subsystems, such as a throwaway database or a local server process, never mock frameworks; line coverage reaches a floor, 60 % by default; end-to-end tests consume the built artifact and leave fresh output; no temporary probe line (tagged vae:probe) remains; no new project adds a lockfile of a package manager other than bun or uv; .env.example lists every configuration key the code reads; and every changed documentation page passes the prose check. A check that cannot fail is not evidence: plain oxlint exits 0 on findings, so the stack defaults call it with --deny-warnings.

Each project owns its policy in .agents/VERIFY.py: the command behind each verb, the thresholds and deterministic rules (a command that must succeed, a file that must exist, text or a pattern a file must or must not contain). The agent extends it, so a defect class that can recur becomes a rule or a test that every later gate enforces. Because the gate runs at every stop, its cost matters. Results are cached under two keys, code plus policy for the suites and pages plus policy for the page checks, so a typo fixed in a page after green suites reruns only the page checks. VERIFIED (defuss-vae README, make bench on release 0.6.0, Apple M4) A gate with nothing changed takes 91 ms (median of seven runs); the hook that inspects every shell command takes 18 ms, 14 ms of it Python start-up.

2.2 Skills and who starts them

The skills are prompts, named as verbs in workflow order. plan traces the code path, probes unknowns and writes a plan to plans/ in which every acceptance criterion is an executable check. implement writes the minimum code against real tests and loops the gate. verify is a deep review against requirements, callers and tests at a goal or a milestone. doc writes documentation pages and doc-edit revises named ones, both ending in a review the program drives (section 2.4). status reconciles the registry of running sub-agents with the process table. wrap splits the work into Conventional Commits, writes the changelog and settles the lessons. A skill loads in full on every invocation, so tests cap each at 6 KiB and all seven at 28 KiB.

Who may start a skill is policy, and code enforces it. The agent starts six skills when the condition in the skill's description holds: plan, for example, only for a risky task that arrived without a plan, after which it stops for review. Only a person starts wrap, because it commits and decides what the project remembers. Claude Code and Codex each read a manifest switch for this, vae.py doctor fails when either switch deviates, and the sub-agent launcher refuses a command that names wrap. Two rules in plan and implement govern structure rather than process: one owner module per concern, which every other module asks; and every contract between modules explicit and checked by a type, a test or a rule. Section 5.10 explains why the case study depends on them.

2.3 Memory in the repository

Failures become episodes; wrap turns each lesson into a test, a rule or a line in a short memory file, and a hook injects that file into every session. Lessons rank by strength: an executable check > a memory line > an episode line. A program enforces the strongest form, so it holds whether or not the agent remembers it.

VERIFIED (defuss-vae 0.8.0 source) The state lives in .agents/. MEMORY.md holds one line per durable decision, each with its reason after BC, at most 240 characters per line and 4 KiB in all. CLI_GIST.md holds the shortest working commands, tagged VERIFIED only after an observed success, at most 2 KiB. The gate writes FAIL, DONE and FINDING lines to EPISODES.md; past 100 entries it trims only its own oldest records, never an open lead, and doctor fails above 30 leads. Session start, and every context compaction, injects the rules, the live sub-agents, the memory, the command gist, the defaults of the stacks the repository uses and the three newest open leads, cut by priority at 9,000 characters, below Claude Code's 10,000-character limit for hook output.

A memory entry binds only within its [scope], the narrowest boundary its evidence supports, and the current request outranks it; repetition, recency and confident wording widen nothing. The rule follows Ning et al. (MemAdapter, 2026), who report that stored memories can make an agent over-align with a user's past beliefs, including inaccurate ones. defuss-vae adopts the principle and leaves out the pipeline: MemAdapter adds three reasoning stages to every retrieval, while a few kilobytes of tagged lines need one rule. wrap audits every entry against the current code and deletes or rewrites one only with evidence; an entry it cannot settle stays, tagged UNKNOWN. The agent may add a rule to AGENTS.md to prevent a repeated mistake and removes its own rule once a test enforces it; it never deletes what a person wrote.

2.4 Checked prose

defuss-vae gates documentation pages like code, in two parts: a static checker enforces typography and document-integrity rules, and a separate review evaluates evidence, reasoning, relevance, structure and language. VERIFIED (defuss-vae 0.8.0 source) The static check runs on every changed page and flags em dashes and spaced en dashes, typographic quotes, the ellipsis character, invisible and look-alike characters, broken links, unclosed fences, leftover placeholders and Mermaid diagrams that would not render. A flagged dash is rewritten by meaning, as a comma, a colon, parentheses or two sentences, never swapped for another character.

The review follows a catalog of 58 rules in seven groups: the evidence and scope of claims, logic, terms, relevance, structure, language and typography. The rules ask whether a claim has its evidence, whether a conclusion follows, whether a number has its base, and whether a page narrates change instead of stating what is. vae.py prose --walk drives that review one part of the page at a time: each step prints the part, the part before it as context, the rules, the static findings in that part and the command for the next step, until the page passes the static check and the walk prints VERIFIED[walk]. That tag records that every part of the page was presented with every rule; it does not establish that each judgment made during the review was correct (section 7).

VERIFIED At the last commit before the session of section 5.6 (2026-10-06), the static check found 380 findings in this repository's 605 documentation pages: 198 dashes (191 em dashes, 7 spaced en dashes), 181 typographic characters (132 ellipsis characters, 37 curly apostrophes, 12 curly quotes) and one broken link, so 379 of the 380 were typography. After that session's documentation pass it found none. Clearing them shows conformity to the typography rules and one repaired link; it does not show that formulaic rhetoric, redundancy or unsupported certainty decreased. This report still contained all three after it had passed the static check and the walk (section 7).

3VAE-DIALECT

VAE-DIALECT is a superset of technical English for agent output and for the skills themselves, designed to reduce token use while preserving meaning. This report does not measure its token savings or its decoding error rate. Its rule of precedence is correctness > compression. Its core is three epistemic tags that never mix:

  • VERIFIED[scope] Established by direct inspection, command output, a test, a measurement or a named authoritative source. Evidence older than the last relevant edit is stale.
  • HYPOTHESIS[scope] A testable inference not yet established, with the cheapest discriminating test or falsifier when it matters.
  • UNKNOWN[scope] A material fact the available evidence does not establish, naming the missing evidence. P=? marks an unknown value.

Confident wording never promotes a hypothesis. On top of the tags, a small operator grammar replaces whole phrases. Operators are exact uppercase words, and every other uppercase word is forbidden, so an operator is never ambiguous:

The skills are written in the dialect, and under the size limits of section 2.2 every rule has to pay for its tokens. VERIFIED (defuss-vae 0.8.0, tests/test_package.py) A test fails on any uppercase word in a skill's prose that is neither an operator nor a listed identifier, and on any WHEN outside the core definition, because WHEN ... THEN reads as a conditional in English while the grammar defines WHEN as equivalence.

The choice of uppercase rests on a hypothesis. HYPOTHESIS Uppercase operators hold a model's attention where the logic of a sentence sits, so an operator is read as an operator. Dillitzer et al. (Attention is Case-Sensitive, 2026) support the mechanism: across 13 models, uppercase spans in lowercase text drew the model's attention to them, consistently in every non-reasoning model they evaluated. They also bound it: more concentrated attention did not by itself raise accuracy, and the thinking phase of reasoning models largely cancelled the effect. The study therefore supports that the operators are noticed, not that they are understood better. Falsifier: on a reasoning and on a non-reasoning model, operators are misread no less often in uppercase than in lowercase.

The losslessness rule makes the dialect more than shorthand. Before emitting compressed text, the writer expands it mentally; if the expansion is not unique, or loses more than negligible meaning, the writer uses the shortest longer form that is unique. A report in the dialect reads like this:

VERIFIED[bundle] BC `bun tests/e2e/scaffold-lean.e2e.ts` → 6/6 apps render as on all.css + all.js
HYPOTHESIS[leak] BC heap +36 MB/page after module release; falsifier=close each happy-dom window, re-measure
UNKNOWN[scaffold-time] BC no timestamps in this repo for the prompts that built the scaffolds
IF HYPOTHESIS[leak] THEN next=cap heap at 4 GB, probe ELSE next=bisect plugins

HYPOTHESIS The tags account for more of the dialect's benefit than the operators. Test: run a fixed task set with four variants of the instructions (neither, tags only, operators only, both) and count unsupported claims and task errors. The hypothesis fails if the operators alone reduce them as much as the tags alone or more.

4The case: defuss-shadcn

defuss-shadcn is a component system of semantic HTML, modern CSS and plain JavaScript on shadcn/ui's design tokens, with no framework and no build step for consumers. It was forked from codylindley/shadcn-html, which had 55 component folders when its development stopped in April 2026. The fork's first commit is dated 2026-09-05; its components ship as plain JavaScript (dist/components/*/*.js). Aron Homberg SAYS the code base had no Markdown single source of truth, no stable API contract and no morphing DOM reconciliation at the time. During the 33 days it was ported to TypeScript, repackaged and refactored several times.

For most of the period the project applied the method with its own tools, because defuss-vae was first published on 2026-10-01: an instruction file (AGENTS.md, 1,731 lines on 2026-10-07) and a verifier (scripts/verify.ts) that runs at the end of every build. Its gates cover, among others: a 1:1 compile of the sources; the State API every interactive component exposes, with states by name, a store, and a render() that reproduces the authored markup exactly, proven by an end-to-end contract; schemas that match each page's state table row for row; DOM access through one runtime only; screenshots of every declared state in light and dark mode; and every figure a page states, written from its measurement. The same gates run over this page. The screenshots are made for inspection by the agent, itself a vision-language model, which opens them through its harness; this revision of the report checked its rendered charts that way. The verifier checks that every declared state has a current screenshot in both modes. No step compares screenshots with earlier ones, and no gate requires the agent to look at them.

VERIFIED Since 2026-10-06 the defuss-vae gate has wrapped that verifier. The project's .agents/VERIFY.py maps the verbs to the repository's own scripts (lint, the unit suite, coverage, bun run verify and the end-to-end runner, whose log it writes to output/), raises the coverage floor to 70 % and adds one rule: no mock framework in any changed file. The session of sections 5.6 to 5.9 ran under defuss-vae 0.5.3, and its transcript shows 0.5.5 from 17:20 UTC on 2026-10-06; this revision of the report ran under 0.8.0.

5.1 Growth

VERIFIED From git, at the last commit of each calendar week (Monday to Sunday, commit dates in UTC+2): 55 components at the fork, with 5 end-to-end test files at the end of the first day and 56 at the end of the second; 72 components and 75 test files by 2026-09-13; 72 and 78 by 2026-09-20; 77 and 83 by 2026-09-27; 219 and 231 by 2026-10-02; and 231 with 252 at commit 8cecf4b4 on 2026-10-07. Over the same span the unit suite grew from 3 to 36 files, which held 618 tests in their last full run, and the verifier from 33 check groups to 42. Several check groups run over every component, which is why the verifier reports more gates than groups (78 in its recorded run of 2026-10-05).

VERIFIED Across the same commits, 350,331 lines were added to authored files and 80,999 removed (git log --numstat, renames detected; generated output excluded: dist/, docs/, the compiled documentation runtime, the generated skills, lockfiles and screenshots). The first day, 2026-09-05, accounts for 56,640 added lines, mostly the forked codebase entering the repository. The largest days of new work are 2026-10-02 (64,422 lines: the website blocks and the application scaffolds) and 2026-10-06 (58,858 lines, including the work of 2026-10-05, committed after midnight). Removals concentrate in the documentation: 69,338 of the 80,999 removed lines, 35,380 of them on 2026-09-11, when the static HTML pages moved to an MDX site generator. Tests grew by 57,578 lines and components by 99,100, about 58 test lines per 100 component lines.

5.2 Review load

VERIFIED On 2026-09-07 the maintainer reviewed the documentation site by hand and filed 52 issues in about eight hours: wrong corners, missing examples, unannounced field hints, dead links. 18 were closed within twelve hours; the fix commits name their issues (fix(select): ... (issue #32)). The rest were closed in one batch on 2026-09-28, so for those the close date is an upper bound, not the fix date.

That sweep is the human review the method budgets for: one person judging what the gates cannot, such as whether a corner looks right, instead of re-checking what they can. HYPOTHESIS The review effort per component falls as the gates grow, because each class of defect found by hand becomes a gate. Falsifier: review time per new component, measured under comparable review conditions, that does not fall across sweeps. Issue counts do not measure effort, and one sweep is not enough data to decide.

5.3 What it ships

Every component is measured on each build: 169 of 232 need no JavaScript. The whole system is 278.2 KiB as one bundle, minified and gzipped, and an application ships a fraction of it. Each application scaffold is bundled on its own, from the core plus only the components its markup uses, and an end-to-end test proves that every scaffold renders on its own bundle exactly as on the full one.

Between the whole system and a single component sit 19 section bundles, one per sidebar section, each holding only its members and loaded after the shared code. They range from 1.9 to 59.1 KiB, 15.3 KiB on average (minified and gzipped).

5.4 Generation speed

HYPOTHESIS Current frontier models build such applications quickly because the system gives them good examples (every component page is executable documentation) and clear instructions (one skill per component), and because the gate turns their mistakes into fix lines instead of silent drift. Test: the same prompts to the same models without the component skills and without the verifier, timed and gated the same way. Falsifier: those runs finish as fast and pass the same gates as often. We have not run that comparison.

5.5 Churn

VERIFIED (Table 2) Code that landed mostly stayed. Of the lines added to the components, 5,793 of 99,100 were removed later (5.8 %); for the tests 2,029 of 57,578 (3.5 %), the shared runtime 138 of 3,204 (4.3 %) and the theme 119 of 5,786 (2.1 %); together 8,079 of 165,668, or 4.9 %. The removals lie elsewhere: 69,338 of the 80,999 removed lines are documentation, about half of them from the single day the static pages moved to MDX, a planned migration rather than rework. Among the code, the tooling churns most (17.8 %); it holds the gates themselves, which were rewritten as they grew.

One reason is established, one is not. VERIFIED The architecture is additive: every component is a folder of its own (a skill, a stylesheet, a script) and shared behavior sits in one runtime, so a new component adds files and edits none of its neighbors. HYPOTHESIS The gates keep defects out of commits, so code is not rewritten after it lands: a defect the verifier names is fixed before the commit, not in a follow-up that replaces the first attempt. Falsifier: line survival per commit (the age of each line in git blame) showing a large share of component code replaced within days of landing. A causal test also needs a comparable project without the gates. We have not measured either.

5.6 Change 1: typed API documentation

Growth adds modules. A change that every existing module must follow is harder: a new architectural rule or a general requirement, applied consistently across dozens or hundreds of modules so that the system still scales. The risk is that an agent edits the first modules carefully and the later ones loosely, and that nothing tells it which ones it missed. One session on 2026-10-06 made four such changes in a row under the defuss-vae gate (section 4). Sections 5.6 to 5.9 report them in order, and Table 8 compares them.

The first requirement arrived in two messages: every interactive component documents its API from typed source. That means a TypeScript signature for every member, a table for every argument, a typed and described detail for every event, the configuration each state accepts, and the shared State API (setState, getState, render, the store) typed for each component's own states, checked by the verifier, by the compiler and on every rendered page.

  • VERIFIED By the final green gate all 59 interactive component sources had changed (+3,455 / −408 lines); in all, 246 authored files changed (+7,570 / −1,537, generated output excluded), since the session also built the section bundles and ran a documentation pass. The verifier's API documentation gate reports no gap in any of the 59, and an end-to-end audit opens all 59 pages.
  • VERIFIED A compiler ratchet counts type errors per file and fails when a count rises. It stood at 1,212 before this change and 1,147 after it; section 5.9 reduced the baseline to zero, so any later type error the compiler reports fails the build.
  • VERIFIED The session, up to the request that added this section to the report, took 5.5 hours of wall-clock time (4.8 hours without pauses over 15 minutes), 662 tool calls and 516,020 output tokens, with one compaction of the agent's context; the work continued from the summary without losing the requirement.
  • VERIFIED The end-to-end runner reruns only the files whose inputs changed: 4 of 245 after a fix to two components, 135 after a change that touched every component.

What the session establishes is narrow. VERIFIED A deep, long-running change that every one of 59 modules must follow was made consistently in one agent session, from a requirement stated in prose and without a module done by hand first, while a program checked every module. It was not flawless: the first pass satisfied a gate that checked the sources but not the rendered pages, and a person caught the gap (section 7). HYPOTHESIS The result repeats on other repositories, requirements and models. Falsifier: a change of the same kind under the same kind of gate that ends with modules the gate passes and a reviewer rejects. HYPOTHESIS The session stayed affordable because the end-to-end runner selected tests by changed inputs and the agent's notes and memory are written in VAE-DIALECT. Falsifier: the same session with every test on every step and plain-prose notes, costing no more time or tokens.

VERIFIED (the session transcript and the coverage runs) The second change was requested at 13:08 UTC: the gate's coverage floor stood at 30 %, Vitest measured 31.6 % of lines, and the target was at least 60 %, another change across the whole system. In 20.6 minutes and 39,926 output tokens the agent raised line coverage by 44.0 percentage points, to 75.6 %, so that the suite executes 10,420 more lines (15,880 instead of 5,460), with 147 lines of tests and an 11-line fix. In that window the model re-read 21.6 million tokens of cached context across its calls (the session's own context, served from the prompt cache), took 86 fresh input tokens and wrote 58,198 tokens to the cache. The work went in two steps:

  • VERIFIED Step 1: a state contract over every fixture. The agent did not write a test per uncovered line. Every interactive component already had an end-to-end fixture with every documented configuration. One contract test loads all 63 interactive fixtures (the 59 components' own and four that compose them) in the unit suite and drives every bound element through every declared state: getState(), the store and render() must agree, and an undeclared state name must throw. Four minutes after the request, coverage stood at 66.9 %.
  • VERIFIED The contract test's first run found a defect: 58 of the 59 components passed. The cookie consent's controller replaces el.api and lacked settled(), which the State API promises on every element; the fix took 11 lines.
  • VERIFIED Step 2: every control operated. Asked to go further where it pays most, the agent reused the same fixtures. A second test clicks every control, sends the keys a keyboard user would and edits every field, holding each component to its main error path: no handler throws, no promise rejects unhandled. It passed on its first run, 63 of 63, and lifted lines to 75.6 % and branches from 38.6 % to 50.5 %. The two tests together are 147 lines.
  • VERIFIED Remaining gaps. The largest are the documentation site's own runtime (about 560 lines, not shipped), third-party packages (about 660) and specific paths in a few large components, where each further point costs a test written for one module. Browser-mode coverage counts everything the pages load, third-party packages included (excluding them had no effect in this mode), so the figure is conservative. The gate's floor is 70 %, and it may only rise.

The first change was large in code; this one was large in reach and small in code. HYPOTHESIS It was cheap because the first change had made the contract uniform and complete: every interactive component exposes the same documented State API and has a fixture of every configuration, so two tests reach all of them. Falsifier: a system without such a contract reaching the same coverage at the same cost. The lesson for the method: before writing tests, look for the contract the modules already share and for the fixtures that already exist.

The request arrived at 15:44:52 UTC: the files on disk should read like the documentation's sidebar. That meant a verifier rule that every component's skill names its section in the front matter (section: actions), a folder per section directly under src/components/, and every component moved into its section, so that src/components/button becomes src/components/actions/button. The change is structural and reaches every component and everything that locates one: the build, the bundler, the screenshot tool, the API reader, the e2e planner, the documentation components and the tests.

VERIFIED (the session transcript, git and the gate) In 43.4 minutes and 76,358 output tokens the agent moved all 228 component folders into the sections that list them, made the layout a rule the verifier enforces, and kept every gate green (246 end-to-end files, 570 unit tests, the verifier) without a human correction. In that window the model re-read 56.2 million tokens of cached context, took 172 fresh input tokens and wrote 130,876 tokens to the cache.

  • VERIFIED Intermediate failures. Each half-done state the agent reached failed by name. Git refused to move questionnaire into a section of the same name. The section plan read the half-moved tree and listed the new folders as components. The statistics crashed reading the flat dist/ through the new helper. The link gate found 481 dead links, 253 between skills and 228 in the generated index; the plugin's prose check refused an exception for the index, so the links were fixed at the source and flattened on the way to dist/. The type checker caught test fixtures without the new key, and the configuration check caught two environment variables the touched scripts read. Each was fixed before the gate turned green.
  • VERIFIED Negative cases. A component without section:, a component in the wrong section and a component outside any section each fail the component sections gate, which names the git mv or the front-matter line that fixes it (a probe; tests/component-sections.test.ts pins each case).
  • VERIFIED Shipped files. The minified sizes and the published paths stayed the same; only the unminified bundle grew, by 0.6 KiB, because its comments name the longer source paths.

HYPOTHESIS A structural change across every module is cheap when one module owns the structure and every other asks it, and safe when the gates turn each half-done state into a named failure instead of a silent one: the agent never had to remember what it had not moved yet. Falsifier: the same move without the gates, or with each tool joining its own paths, completing as fast and leaving no tool that still looks in the old place.

The fourth change began at 17:29:02 UTC, directly after the third: remove the type errors the ratchet had counted since the first change, and measure again. Until then every written type was checked only against a baseline that could fall and never rise. The third change had moved the code; this one changed its types, and it was not allowed to change what runs. A type is erased by the build, so the shipped bytes are the proof.

VERIFIED (the session transcript, git, the compiler, cmp and the gate) In 12.5 minutes and 71,958 output tokens the agent removed all 1,147 type errors the ratchet had carried in 52 component files. After 27.3 minutes and 82,855 tokens every gate was green again (the verifier, 571 unit tests, 246 end-to-end files), and the 85 minified files the system ships were byte-identical to the previous build, without a human correction. Up to zero errors the model re-read 79.3 million tokens of cached context, took 178 fresh input tokens and wrote 135,450 tokens to the cache; up to the green gates, 91.6 million, 236 and 225,359.

  • VERIFIED The shared query module. Every component selects the DOM through one shared module. Typing what it returns there (an HTMLElement by default, the named element for a tag selector) removed 707 of the 1,147 errors, as a probe on the previous commit plus that one file showed. The other 440 were local: optional parameters, event targets, the shape of a state declared where it grows.
  • VERIFIED A bundling defect found by byte comparison. After the edits, the Notes app's bundle differed from the previous build. The bundler finds the components an app needs by reading the source for their init calls, and dfDollar<HTMLDialogElement>('dialog:not(...)') no longer matched, so the Notes app would have shipped without the dialog script. Two verifier checks read the source the same way and failed by name: the State API marker for the tree view and the dialog ownership boundary. All three have accepted a type argument since then, and tests/apps.test.ts pins the bundler's case. UNKNOWN Whether an end-to-end test would have caught the missing script: the broken bundle never ran.
  • VERIFIED A type corrected by the compiler. The agent first typed the calendar's selected day as a string; the next compile named every place that calculates with it, and the type became number | null.

Two lessons for the method follow. When a change must not alter behavior, compare the shipped bytes as well as running the tests; here the comparison was the only check that saw the missing script. And a tool that reads source as text is a parser of the language: new syntax in the source, here a type argument, is new input for every such tool.

HYPOTHESIS The fourth change was fast for the reason the third was: one module owns what every query returns, so a type fixed there is fixed in every component that asks it. Falsifier: removing the same errors component by component, without the shared fix, at no more edits per error.

5.10 Small modules, explicit contracts

HYPOTHESIS VAE works here because every module stands on its own. Small, independent modules (components, micro-frontends, microservices) suit an agent better than a person: a person loses track among hundreds of components, while an agent reads any one of them in full and a gate checks all of them on every run. The agent does not need to hold the whole system in mind, and it did not (this session's context was compacted once): each module can be read alone, and the gate covers the whole. The risk sits between modules. Where a contract between two of them is implicit or keeps changing, a test the agent saw green can turn red after the next, unrelated change, and nothing names the dependency that broke. Under VAE, separation of concerns, explicit contracts, small modules and composition over inheritance or shared state therefore decide whether a green gate means anything.

  • VERIFIED Explicit contracts. Every component is a folder of its own, and every interactive one exposes a contract a program checks: states by name, a store, a render() that reproduces its markup, a schema, a typed API. Because each end-to-end test's inputs are explicit, the runner can select the tests a change affects: 4 of 245 after a fix to two components.
  • VERIFIED Failures between modules. Three failures came from the gaps between modules. The documentation's search palette stopped working because the dialog script claimed a <dialog> that another component owned; that ownership is an explicit rule and a gate. In the session of section 5.6, the tabs script claimed the BibTeX component's tab list, which surfaced only when each section was bundled on its own. And every live example made the page recalculate its styles once per example, a cost no single module showed, only many of them on one page (section 6).

Falsifier: changes that cross module boundaries breaking green tests no more often than changes inside one module. The repository can measure this, by finding the commits that fix a test an earlier commit left green and counting the component folders each touches; we have not measured it.

5.11 The cost of a long instruction file

VERIFIED (the session transcript; Figure 8) The instruction file has 1,731 lines. In the session that wrote the first version of this report, the first request wrote 69,980 tokens of instructions, rules and memory to the prompt cache, and later requests read them back from it. Up to the commit that added this measurement (2026-10-07), 580.7 million input tokens were cache reads, 2.6 million were cache writes and 2,330 were uncached: 99.6 % of all input came from the cache. Anthropic's prompt-caching pricing bills a cache read at a tenth of the price of an uncached input token, so in this session most of the instruction file's cost per request was billed at the cache-read rate. The accounting covers tokens only. It does not cover copies of the file that drift (section 10), or the maintenance each added component brings: screenshots, gates and tests for as long as it exists.

6Anecdotes: self-correction

This section and the next report cases from a few sessions, chosen because each shows a mechanism; they are not counted or sampled. The representative evidence is section 5, measured over every component on every build. The cases below show the agent correcting itself, prompted by a rule or a check rather than by a person. Agents in VAE sessions narrate such corrections; this one is from a session on the defuss-vae README:

One more README claim is too absolute: "no program can" check e2e coverage. Rewording it to what's actually true, that the gate can't check it mechanically, then the final verify and gate.

No check would have failed on the original sentence; the correction follows the rule that every material claim carries its evidence. From the sessions that wrote this report, each with its evidence:

  • The lean bundles were wrong at first. The test that compares each app on its own bundle with the full system found 105 elements rendering differently: icon sizing that lives on an attribute selector, the typography baseline on body, generated ids. The resolver was fixed until all six apps matched.
  • A claim met its measurement. The flagship deck said verification takes "≈ 4 min". Timed, the verifier alone takes 10.2 s; four minutes was the whole pipeline. The slide cites a recorded run, and a gate checks it.
  • A timeout was a performance bug. In the session of section 5.6 a unit test timed out in two of three runs. A CPU profile, instead of a longer timeout, showed that every live example measured its layout right after writing styles, forcing a style recalculation of the whole page per example: 6.4 s on a page with twelve. Batched, it took 1.75 s, and an end-to-end check counts the forced recalculations.
  • A contract caught a state. The BibTeX component's render contract failed because getState() did not report the format on show after a copy. One line in its read() fixed it; without the contract the gap would have stayed hidden until a tool relied on it.

7Anecdotes: what the gates missed

Like section 6, these are cases, not a census. The gates check correctness against what is specified; they do not check cost, look and feel, or taste. In this period a person, and once a clean machine, found each of the following:

  • A build froze the machine. A full pipeline run made a 24 GB laptop unresponsive. The static-site renderer created a happy-dom window per page and never closed it, under a 14 GB heap allowance. Closing each window after its page is written took the heap from 4 GB in 17 s (a crash at the cap) to a flat 48 MB; the build runs under a 2 GB cap that fails instead of swapping.
  • Animations ran instantly. The minifier rewrote 2600ms as 2.6s, and the diagram engine read it as 2.6 ms. Every test passed, because none asserted the timing a person sees.
  • A number in a brief. The brief for this report said the system grew "from 20 to more than 200 components". Git and the upstream repository say 55. The measured number went into the report; the recollection did not.
  • Done after one page. In the session of section 5.6 the gate passed and the agent reported the typed API documentation complete; the maintainer opened another page and found the configuration of each state missing. The gate checked the sources, not what every page shows, and the correction became an end-to-end audit of all 59 pages.
  • A clean CI runner. Every gate before 2026-10-06 had passed on the maintainer's laptop. The first CI runs on a clean runner, that day, found two dependencies on that machine within an hour. Run 1: lint, unit tests and screenshots passed, and verify failed its stats.json freshness check, because the file records gzip sizes and the Bun declared in package.json (1.3.9) compresses the bundle to 139,902 bytes where the Bun that builds it (1.4.2) gives 140,945. Run 2, with the versions aligned: two of 564 unit tests timed out on the slower runner, because their hang guards were sized for a laptop; CI scales them since. Run 3 passed, 14:16 to 14:36 UTC.
  • Defects seen on screen. On 2026-10-07 the maintainer reported five defects that showed only on screen, in one session (.agents/EPISODES.md): toolbar toggles and dark-mode surfaces in the Document Editor, diagram wires that lagged and jumped on slides, a slide that flickered at about 3 Hz, two-line captions in this report set off-center, and a rotating glyph that aliased mid-turn. Four became end-to-end checks the same day. The fifth remains an open lead, because its edges were measured only in a still frame, never during the motion.
  • Rhetoric that passed the prose checks. After this report had passed the static check and the walk, a separate editorial review supplied by the maintainer found sweeping guarantees, falsifiers that did not falsify their claims, and testimonial passages in the agent's section. The static check enforces typography and document integrity, and the walk records only that a guided review was completed. This revision applies that review.

Each of these became a guard afterwards: a heap cap and a benchmark target that keeps measurement out of the regular pipeline, a unit-aware timing parser with a test, a gate that ties every figure to its measurement, an audit of every page, scaled hang guards on CI, and four new end-to-end checks.

8History of the method

VERIFIED The verifier and the instruction file are both in the fork's first commit on 2026-09-05, and the verifier grew with the system (section 5.1). The method was then generalized as defuss-vae, first published on 2026-10-01. The general package changed quickly: 56 commits and 13 further releases from 0.3.0 (2026-10-03) to 0.8.0 (2026-10-07). Documentation pages are gated from 0.4.0, the notation is named VAE-DIALECT from 0.5.0, 0.6.0 renamed the skills to verbs and added the sub-agent registry, 0.7.0 let the agent start six of the seven skills, and 0.8.0 added the page walk. On 2026-10-06 the package returned to the project it came from: its gate wraps the project's own verifier (section 4), which remains the authority on everything specific to the component system.

Lessons travel in both directions. VERIFIED Section 5.9 ends with two of them: compare the shipped bytes when a change must not alter behavior, and treat every tool that reads source as text as a parser. Both appear as steps of the implement skill in defuss-vae 0.6.0, released the next day. The rule of one owner module per concern entered this repository's AGENTS.md at 04:38 UTC on 2026-10-07 and the plan and implement skills of 0.6.0 at 08:49 UTC the same day.

9Limitations

The study covers one project, one maintainer, one family of models and 33 days, without a control group. For most of the period the project used only its own verifier. The defuss-vae gate has wrapped it since 2026-10-06, so the evidence for the package itself is two days of sessions under 0.5.3 and 0.5.5 plus this revision under 0.8.0; the features of 0.6.0 to 0.8.0 (agent-started skills, the sub-agent registry, the page walk) are described here from their source, not measured. Issue counts and commit counts are proxies, and the scaffold timings are an account, not a measurement. Until 2026-10-06 the repository had no CI, so every earlier green gate ran on one machine, and the first CI runs found two dependencies on it (section 7). An attestation records a claim that a review occurred; it does not establish the review's completeness or quality. A gate rewards what it measures, and an agent under pressure can satisfy a check by weakening it. The instruction file forbids loosening a schema to pass, but that rule is prose, the form the method itself treats as unenforced.

10The agent's account

This section is written in the first person by Claude (Opus 5.5), the agent that drafted the report. It is limited to observations from its own sessions.

  • In the session of section 5.6 I reported the API documentation complete after checking one page; section 7 describes the gap and the audit that closed it.
  • The verifier's fix lines named my next command. A figure that disagreed with its measurement failed with "run bun scripts/stat-figures.ts, then rebuild the docs", and that command resolved it.
  • Mid-task, I was handed an outdated copy of the instruction file.
  • The pipeline run that froze the maintainer's laptop (section 7) was one I started; no gate measured machine load.
  • Repository files preserve selected context across my sessions: on 2026-10-07 .agents/MEMORY.md held eight entries, 2.3 of its 4 KiB. UNKNOWN How this behaves in other harnesses; I observed it in Claude Code only.

11Conclusion

Over 33 days defuss-shadcn grew from 55 to 232 components while a deterministic verifier checked the conventions encoded in its rules on every build, and a person reviewed what those rules do not cover, such as appearance. The failures in section 7 lay outside the rules (machine load, timing a person sees, a remembered number, the rendered pages, a second machine, the rhetoric of this report); most led to a new check or guard, one is an open lead, and the rhetoric was revised after an editorial review. In one session a requirement was applied to all 59 interactive components, and the verifier's documentation gate confirmed it for every component after one human correction extended the check to the rendered pages. The study covers one project and one maintainer and has no control group. Whether the results generalize is open; the comparison named in section 5.4 is the next step.

12Future research

Each question below is raised and left open by this report; each names the measurement that would answer it.

  1. Stability of the method. Does a deep change like that of section 5.6 succeed again, on other repositories, requirements and models, and how often does the first pass fall short, as it did here? Measure line survival per commit (section 5.5), cross-module test failures (section 5.10) and human review effort per component (section 5.2) over several months.
  2. Token efficiency of VAE-DIALECT. How many tokens do the tags and the operator grammar save, and at what cost in errors? Compare uppercase, lowercase and no operators on reasoning and non-reasoning models (section 3), with the session totals of section 5.6 as a baseline.
  3. Parallel agents. defuss-vae 0.6.0 added a registry that gives each sub-agent its own git worktree and refuses overlapping claims; no session in this report used it. When modules compose through explicit contracts, can several agents work at once, each owning a set of modules? Measure merge conflicts, contract drift and green gates that turn red after a merge.
  4. Cost as a gated property. No gate in this report measured machine load, wall time or tokens, and a pipeline run froze the maintainer's laptop (section 7). Record heap, wall time and tokens per gate run, set limits, and measure how often a limit fails a change that every correctness gate passes.
  5. Who starts a skill. Since 0.7.0 the agent starts six of the seven skills itself. Measure how often it starts each one, whether it skips the deep review at milestones, and how many human prompts a task needs, against sessions in which a person starts every skill.
  6. More languages, frameworks and setups. This report covers one HTML, CSS and TypeScript system, one maintainer and one harness. defuss-vae ships defaults for Go, Rust, the JVM, .NET, JavaScript and Python; apply the method to back-end services, data pipelines and teams under the same gates and measurements.
